title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 12 (27/06/2019)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 27 JUNE 2019
Subject: The Claimant filed two challenges to the Sole Arbitrator (selected by the LCIA
Court) pursuant to Article 10.3 of the LCIA Rules 2014.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: London, England
Governing Law of English law
the Contract:
Summary: The first challenge (First Challenge) related mainly to the Sole Arbitrator’s
dismissal of the Claimant’s application for interim measures. The Claimant
(self-represented) argued that the Sole Arbitrator: (i) failed to consider the
submissions made in the application; (ii) failed to resolve the issues on which
the application turned; (iii) failed to take a balanced approach to procedural
issues; (iv) had not maintained the required level of fairness between the
Parties; (v) was heavily influenced by the submissions made by the
Respondent; and (vi) refused to hear the application urgently.
The second challenge (Second Challenge) related to: (i) the Sole Arbitrator’s
response to the First Challenge; and (ii) alleged misrepresentations in the Sole
Arbitrator’s curriculum vitae regarding prior experience sitting as an
arbitrator.
The LCIA Court rejected both challenges in a single decision.
The LCIA Court applied English law (the law of the seat).
The conduct of the Sole Arbitrator prior to the hearing on interim measures
was clearly a matter which fell outside the 14-day period prescribed under
Article 10.3 of the LCIA Rules. The Claimant was content to proceed without
notifying any challenge up to the hearing on interim measures.
The Claimant’s allegations relating to the Sole Arbitrator’s decision on the
application for interim measures comprised nothing more than a series of
complaints that the Sole Arbitrator preferred the submissions and contentions
of the Respondent, without any specific evidence of lack of impartiality or
independence. The Claimant’s allegation that the Sole Arbitrator failed to give
“any proper consideration to the Claimant’s asserted intellectual property
rights in the decision” was merely a reflection of the fact that the relief
requested was refused.
The Arbitrator had no power, in the context of an application for interim

measures, to resolve the merits of the dispute and could only, at the highest,
grant an injunction on an interim basis to restrain the Respondent’s conduct.
That application failed on the conventional grounds that the Claimant had not
established that the application was urgent or that substantial prejudice
would be suffered if interim relief was not granted, and there was nothing to
indicate that the Sole Arbitrator conducted the analysis of these issues in
anything other than a diligent and professional manner.
The First Challenge therefore amounted to an attempt to appeal or overturn
the Sole Arbitrator’s decision on the application for interim measures and had
to be dismissed.
The Sole Arbitrator’s response to the First Challenge, objecting strongly to any
suggestion of lack of competence, even if unnecessarily strident, did not
suggest an inability to continue to act in an independent and unbiased
manner.
The matters regarding the Sole Arbitrator’s limited or non-existent previous
arbitrator experience, and the alleged CV-related misrepresentations
regarding the Sole Arbitrator’s experience were known to the Claimant
months before it filed the Second Challenge and are therefore barred by the
14-day deadline in Article 10.3 of the LCIA Rules. In any event, lack of prior
experience sitting as arbitrator is not a proper ground for a challenge based
on Article 10.2 of the LCIA Rules without evidence of lack of fairness or
impartiality or other questionable conduct.
Decision 12 - 2

London Court of International Arbitration
Arbitration No: […]
B E TW E E N
[…]
Claimant
-and-
[…]
Respondent
_______________________________________________________
DECISION ON TWO CHALLENGES TO SOLE ARBITRATOR
_______________________________________________________
Parties
1. The Claimant is […] a company incorporated in the United Kingdom. It is represented internally
by [Employee A] and externally by [Law Firm A] in London, UK.
2. The Respondent is […] an organisation based in Belgium. The Respondent is represented by
[Law Firm B] in Brussels, Belgium. [Party A] and [Party B] are also related to this matter.
Background to the Dispute
3. The dispute between the parties arises out of a license agreement dated 31 August 2017 (the
Agreement), by which the Respondent agreed to license from the Claimant the right to use
[the Claimant’s] Digital Platform in order to create, operate, maintain, host, market and
promote a new mobile app to be designed by the Claimant […] (the […] App).
Decision 12 - 3

4. The […] App was to be designed by the Claimant to mirror its previous app […]. The Claimant
secured funding for the Respondent from [Party B] in the sum of €115,769 to be paid to the
Claimant to build and manage the app.
5. The Claimant alleges that the Agreement restricted the ability of the Respondent to create a
similar or competing app to the […] App. The app was publicly launched […].
6. In June 2018, the Respondent advised the Claimant orally that it did not intend to pay the
remaining balance due for the app and that it would terminate the contract and hire a
developer to create a new version of the app. The Respondent failed to pay an invoice in the
amount of €18,687.27.
7. On 13 July 2018, the Respondent sent a termination letter to the Claimant relying on Clause
15A of the Agreement as a basis for termination, alleging that the Claimant had breached
Clause 16A of the Agreement by disparaging the Respondent and by failing timely to provide
the agreed functionalities of the app. The Claimant, conversely, contends that the termination
was ineffective in that the Respondent failed to identify any breach of the Agreement, failed
to identify whether the breach was remediable and failed to allow the Claimant 30 days to
remedy the breach.
8. The Claimant filed a Request for Arbitration in 16 November 2018 in which it seeks: (i) the
payment of the balance of fees owing, in the sum of €51,061.81, (ii) damages in the amount
of €115,000; (iii) a declaration that the intellectual property rights in the […] app and content
management system remain the Claimant’s property; and (iv) interest and costs.
9. The Respondent filed a Response and counterclaim on 14 December 2018. The Respondent
contends that the Claimant failed to comply with its obligations and failed to deliver the app
with the agreed functionalities within the contractual time limits. The Respondent contends
that the Claimant’s breaches gave rise to the right to terminate the Agreement, which it did
duly and lawfully. The Respondent states that during the development of the app, it incurred
Decision 12 - 4

significant costs, which were lost as a consequence of the Claimant’s breaches. The
Respondent therefore claims these losses, in an estimated amount of €20,000.
10. [Arbitrator A] was appointed as sole arbitrator on 29 November 2018. She held a procedural
conference call on 10 January 2019 and set the timetable for the arbitration on 11 January
2019.
Application for interim measures
11. On 21 December 2018, the Claimant submitted a request for interim measures (RIM) under
Article 25 of the LCIA Rules. In its application, the Claimant requested that the arbitrator:
• order the Respondent to stop all work on any app related to the app owned by the
Claimant;
• order the Respondent to disclose to the Claimant copies of communication with
software developers regarding the creation or development of a related app;
• order the Respondent to take down all content and reference to the app on their
website.
12. The Respondent submitted a response to the RIM on 18 January 2019 in which it denied the
Claimant’s requests, on the basis that:
• the request for interim measures is grounded in a platform agreement over which the
arbitrator has no jurisdiction;
• the alleged claim for breach of IP does not meet a prima facie case of validity on the
merits;
• the Claimant has not provided evidence of a breach by the Respondent of the
Claimant’s IP rights; and
• the requested relief presents no urgency and the Claimant has not submitted
evidence on how any delay in issuing it would cause irreparable damage.
Decision 12 - 5

13. A hearing on the RIM took place on 8 March 2019, following which the arbitrator issued a
decision, on 27 March 2019, in which she dismissed the application on the grounds that the
Claimant had not established that the application was urgent or that substantial prejudice
would be suffered if interim relief was not granted. In her decision, the arbitrator expressed
her concerns about the escalating costs of the matter and invited the parties to attempt to
settle the dispute amicably.
14. By email dated 2 April 2019, the parties agreed to stay the proceedings to attempt amicable
resolution of the dispute.
The Challenges
15. By attachments to an email dated 11 April 2019, the Claimant submitted a challenge to the
arbitrator pursuant to Article 10.1 of the LCIA Arbitration Rules.
16. The challenge is made, in summary, on the following grounds:
(i) In her decision dated 27 March 2019, the arbitrator failed to consider the submissions
made in the application for interim measures and failed to resolve the issues on
which the request for interim measures turned. This resulted in the Claimant’s
intellectual property rights being ignored without proper consideration.
(ii) The arbitrator failed to take a balanced approach to procedural issues and has not
maintained the required level of fairness between the parties. The Claimant relies on
the history of the arbitrator’s treatment of the parties and alleges that she was
heavily influenced by the submissions made by the Respondent.
(iii) The arbitrator had refused to hear the Claimant’s early application for interim
measures urgently.
17. The challenge was accompanied by a Chronology of relevant events and a Challenge Bundle
of documents containing all or most of the papers in the arbitration.
Decision 12 - 6

18. By email of 19 April 2019, the arbitrator informed the LCIA that she did not intend to resign.
19. By email dated 25 April 2019, the Respondent served a Response to the challenge. In its
Response the Respondent states, in summary, that:
• the challenge was filed outside of the time limit provided by Article 10.3 of the Rules
and should therefore be dismissed.
• the challenge was filed as an attempt to obtain interim relief where it has already
been denied by the arbitrator;
The Response was accompanied by a paginated list of exhibits.
20. By email dated 29 April 2019, the arbitrator confirmed to the parties that she would not resign
and responded to the challenge in the following terms:
1. I refute any allegations of bias or impartiality . On the contrary, I have tried very
hard to give the Claimant time to make all her arguments as fully as she wishes
recognising her position as a litigant in person and I have listened and understood
these arguments. I have acceded to requests for more time from the Claimant and
postponed the first hearing at the Claimant's request despite the Respondent
objecting due to a member of their team not being available . As part of the Interim
measures decision I have not made any findings on the merits of the substantive
case and indeed have accepted that there may be a prima facie case to answer on
the claims . However I found that the grounds for interim measures had not been
made out .
2. In so far as allegations against me regarding my competence, I simply point out
that I have been a qualified lawyer for [many] years; undertaken many LCIA
arbitrations as counsel and have been familiar with their rules for many years now .
Further, I was a […] partner […] and understand well the IP issues in this matter . I
object strongly therefore to any suggestions that I lack competence to hear the case .
Decision 12 - 7

Finally, my resume was before the parties on my appointment last year and no
objections were taken as to my competence at that stage.”
21. On 23 May 2019 the LCIA Secretariat notified the parties of the appointment of the
undersigned […] to determine the challenge. On 24 May 2019 the parties were informed that
I would also determine the second challenge referred to below.
22. On 26 April 2019 the Claimant sought to file a Reply to the response, for which the Rules made
no provision. By email dated 28 May 2019 I granted permission to file the Reply to which I
would attach such weight as I deemed appropriate.
23. On 7 May 2019 the Claimant filed a second challenge based, inter alia, on the following
grounds:
(i) The arbitrator’s response to the first challenge gives rise to justifiable doubts as to her
impartiality or independence, and the LCIA Court should conclude that the arbitrator
is unfit to act because she has not acted fairly or impartially as between the parties
by her response to the first challenge.
(ii) In her curriculum vitae, the arbitrator made a false or misleading statement regarding
her experience, by representing that she had previously been appointed and/or acted
as arbitrator in one or more arbitrations when in fact at the date of appointment she
had never done so.
The second Challenge was accompanied by a bundle of documents relevant to the challenge.
24. On 21 May 2019 the Respondent served a response to the second challenge requesting that
the challenged be dismissed and the claimant be ordered to pay the costs.
25. On 28 May 2019 the Claimant served a reply to the Response to the second challenge.
Decision 12 - 8

26. The parties, in the course of the above submissions and applications have referred to and
provided copies of numerous authorities including previous decisions of the LCIA Court on
challenges. All such authorities have been reviewed but only those considered relevant and
necessary to the decision are cited in this decision. Likewise the parties have referred to a
very large number of documents including communications passing between them, the
arbitrator and/or the LCIA. Only those considered relevant are cited in this decision.
Applicable Rules
27. The relevant provisions of the LCIA Rules are as follows:
Article 10 Revocation and Challenges
10.1 The LCIA Court may revoke any arbitrator’s appointment upon its own initiative,
at the written request of all other members of the Arbitral Tribunal or upon a written
challenge by any party if: (i) that arbitrator gives written notice to the LCIA Court of
his or her intent to resign as arbitrator, to be copied to all parties and all other
members of the Arbitral Tribunal (if any); (ii) that arbitrator falls seriously ill, refuses
or becomes unable or unfit to act; or (iii) circumstances exist that give rise to
justifiable doubts as to that arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
10.2 The LCIA Court may determine that an arbitrator is unfit to act under Article 10.1
if that arbitrator: (i) acts in deliberate violation of the Arbitration Agreement; (ii) does
not act fairly or impartially as between the parties; or (iii) does not conduct or
participate in the arbitration with reasonable efficiency, diligence and industry.
10.3 A party challenging an arbitrator under Article 10.1 shall, within 14 days of the
formation of the Arbitral Tribunal or (if later) within 14 days of becoming aware of any
grounds described in Article 10.1 or 10.2, deliver a written statement of the reasons
for its challenge to the LCIA Court, the Arbitral Tribunal and all other parties. A party
may challenge an arbitrator whom it has nominated, or in whose appointment it has
participated, only for reasons of which it becomes aware after the appointment has
been made by the LCIA Court.
10.4 The LCIA Court shall provide to those other parties and the challenged arbitrator
a reasonable opportunity to comment on the challenging party’s written statement.
The LCIA Court may require at any time further information and materials from the
challenging party, the challenged arbitrator, other parties and other members of the
Arbitral Tribunal (if any).
Decision 12 - 9

28. The Claimant relies on Article 10.1(ii) and/or (iii) and cites authorities on the English Common
Law test for apparent bias as well as other published guidance referred to in the challenges
and subsequent submissions.
29. The test in Article 10 of the LCIA Rules, requires that “circumstances exist that give rise to
justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality and independence” [emphasis added]. The
application of the test as set out in the LCIA Rules can be found in some anonymised selected
decisions of the LCIA Court, which are cited and relied on in the papers.
30. A different test is set by Section 24(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act 1996, which provides that
“circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable grounds as to [the arbitrator’s] impartiality.
The application of the Common Law test is referred to in the leading House of Lords case of
Porter v Magill [2001] UK HL 67 where, in relation to the disqualification of the Leader of a
London Council (not a Judge as stated), the House of Lords emphasised that one must first
ascertain all the circumstances bearing on the suggestion of bias and then ask whether those
circumstances would lead a fair-minded and informed observer to conclude that there was a
“real possibility or a real danger, the two being the same, that the Tribunal was biased”. The
same test has recently been applied in the case of an arbitrator in Halliburton v Chubb [2018]
EWCA Civ 817 (although the case is currently on appeal to the Supreme Court) and in a number
of similar authorities and leading textbooks.
31. Ultimately, the question for the Tribunal is whether, in the eyes of the fair-minded and
informed observer, there is a real possibility or a real danger that the person whose conduct
is under challenge is not independent and impartial as between the parties .
32. Also relevant to the present challenges is Article 10.3 and the rule that a challenge must be
delivered within 14 days of becoming aware of any grounds of challenge. The application of
this Rule can be dealt with quite shortly. A dispute has developed between the parties as to
whether the initial challenge served on 11 April was or was not served within 14 days of the
arbitrator’s Decision in the application for Interim Measures, which was dated 27 March 2019.
Depending on how the Rule is to be interpreted, it may be that the 14 days expired on 10
Decision 12 - 10

April. While challenging this conclusion, the Claimant also invites the LCIA Court to exercise
its power under Article 22.5 to extend time if needed.
33. In my view there can be no question that the Claimant’s primary challenge should be
considered on its merits whether or not one day late. However, there is every good reason
why Article 10.3 should be applied to bar a complaint in circumstances where it is clear on the
facts that the challenging party was aware of the grounds being relied on for a period
substantially outside the 14 day period but continued to participate in the arbitration, unless
special circumstances indicate that the rule should be relaxed and the challenged entertained.
These observations apply to both challenges which are now considered separately on their
merits.
First Challenge
34. The first general point to note is that the LCIA Rules require a “written statement of the
reasons for [the] challenge” and for other parties including the challenged arbitrator to have
a “reasonable opportunity to comment” on the challenge. The LCIA Court may then require
further information or materials. The process is clearly not intended to replicate a full
exchange of pleadings or contentions as in the arbitration itself. This reflects the fact that a
high standard of proof is required for an arbitrator to be removed and that the challenge
process is not intended to be a comprehensive review of the conduct of the arbitration.
35. In the present case, the first challenge, although based on reasonably straightforward
grounds, occupies some 28 pages and is accompanied by a bundle of 386 pages plus a
chronology. This has given rise to a response of 18 pages together with exhibits; and, as noted
above, the Claimant was granted leave to serve a reply of 10 pages accompanied by a “reply
bundle”. While there is no limit, express or implied on the volume of material that may be
placed before the Court in pursuit of a challenge this case is unusual in having given rise to
such a large quantity of material concerning relatively straightforward allegations.
36. Turning to the challenge itself, this is expressed in terms of 3 “submissions” which are in
summary that:
Decision 12 - 11

(i) The arbitrator has not treated the parties equally, fairly and impartially in her conduct
of the arbitration, in support of which the Claimant seeks to invoke the full history of
the arbitrator’s treatment of the parties before her decision on interim measures,
delivered on 27 March 2017.
(ii) The arbitrator’s conduct in the hearing of the Claimant’s request for interim measures
on 9 March combined with her treatment of the Claimant’s submissions and evidence
at the hearing, give rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence, specifically in failing to give any or any proper consideration to the
Claimant’s asserted intellectual property rights and the arbitrator’s reliance on the
Respondent’s assertions.
(iii) The arbitrator’s refusal to hear the Claimant’s early application for interim measures
urgently, following objection by the Respondent’s counsel. In the decision the
arbitrator wrongly accepted that the Claimant’s assertion of urgency had not been
made out, showing a failure to treat the parties equally, fairly and impartially.
37. In the Respondent’s response to the challenge the Claimant’s various assertions are
challenged including the Claimant’s account of facts leading up to the application for interim
measures. In this regard, the conduct of the arbitrator prior to the hearing on interim
measures is clearly a matter which falls outside the 14 day period prescribed under the Rules.
The Claimant was content to proceed without notifying any challenge up to the hearing on
interim measures and in my view no case has been advanced and certainly none is made out
for treating the events prior to the hearing on interim measures as in any way exceptional or
such as to invoke a relaxation of Article 10.3 as discussed above.
38. Despite this, one matter which is dealt with in some detail in the submissions is the contended
failure of the arbitrator to deal fairly or properly with the Claimant’s assertion of urgency and
the alleged need for relief to prevent the Respondent benefitting from the Claimant’s IP, in
breach of its contractual obligations. It is said that when the Respondent objected to a prompt
hearing the arbitrator performed a volte-face and the Claimant was thus forced to make the
Decision 12 - 12

separate application for interim relief. As explained in more detail in the Respondent’s
Response, these assertions represent a misunderstanding, perhaps as a result of the Claimant
being represented by its owner without the benefit of legal advice or guidance.
39. In fact, the Claimant had made no application for injunctive relief in its request for arbitration,
which asked only for damages and a declaration. The request did ask that the arbitration be
expedited and as a result on 3 December 2018 the arbitrator wrote to the parties suggesting
the matter be dealt with as a preliminary issue. However, the Respondent (as it was entitled
to) did not agree to this course. Thus, on 5 December 2018 the arbitrator invited the Claimant
to apply for interim relief if it wished to do so. The Claimant eventually did apply for interim
measures by its application dated 21 December 2018. There was no explanation as to the
delay in making this application, but it is clear there was no “volte-face” by the arbitrator,
whose conduct was thus helpful to the Claimant.
40. The arbitrator then gave directions for a Response to the application for interim measures and
for a Reply to the Response to be served on 12 February with a hearing on in the interim
measures application on 15 February 2019. On the 12 February 2019 there was a delay in the
Claimant providing its Reply to the Response on interim measures as a result of which the
Claimant asked for a postponement of the hearing. The arbitrator agreed to the Claimant’s
request so that the hearing was postponed for some 3 weeks to 8 March 2019, despite the
unavailability of one of the Respondent’s Counsel. The hearing duly took place on 8 March
2019 and the decision was delivered 19 days later on 27 March 2019.
41. These details are cited only to make the point that the arbitrator, perhaps as a result of the
Claimant not then being legally represented, had been indulgent to a party asserting the need
for urgent relief. Many arbitrators might have been expected to take a much less indulgent
line with the Claimant.
42. Returning to the core of the Claimant’s complaints which must be taken as grounded in the
decision on interim measures, the Claimant’s assertions can be taken together. They
comprise nothing more than a series of complaints that the arbitrator preferred the
submissions and contentions of the Respondent. Beyond the repeated assertions of a lack of
Decision 12 - 13

impartiality or independence, no specific evidence is presented. The assertion that the
arbitrator failed to give “any or any proper consideration to the Claimant’s asserted
intellectual property rights in the decision” is merely a reflection of the fact that the relief
requested was refused. It may be that the Claimant had misunderstood the purpose and
scope of the application for interim measures and had assumed that the function of the
arbitrator was to render a final decision.
43. It is clear from the Rules that the powers of the arbitrator, as regards the request for Interim
Measures, was limited to making an order “on a provisional basis subject to a final decision in
an award [of] any relief which the arbitral tribunal would have power to grant in an award”.
The arbitrator had no power to give a final decision. It is unclear whether the Claimant
properly appreciated the limited powers in relation to interim measures. The way the
arbitrator dealt with the application in her decision, apparently following the Respondent’s
submission, was to treat the application as being in effect for an injunction. Thus in addition
to showing that damages would not be an adequate remedy, it was necessary for the Claimant
to show that it would suffer substantial prejudice if the interim measure was not granted and
that the balance of convenience favoured the applicant. The arbitrator found that the case
was not made out and that the Claimant had not established the application as urgent.
44. In my view, the decision given on 27 March 2019 was commendable in having dealt with
technically difficult and procedurally complex issues succinctly and in a manner which did
justice to the case of both parties. Perhaps the short point arising from the voluminous
complaints of the Claimant is that it was hoped and expected that the arbitrator, having heard
the issues on an interim basis, would give a decision in the Claimant’s favour as regards the
Respondent’s continued use of the Claimant’s intellectual property, information and rights.
However, it is clear that the procedure adopted by the Claimant itself could not lead to any
meaningful decision in the Claimant’s favour.
45. The question of what relief the arbitrator was asked to grant was entirely a matter for the
Claimant; and if no such relief could be granted within the LCIA Rules that was a matter for
the Claimant and no-one else. The challenge accuses the arbitrator of failing to consider or
resolve the Claimant’s primary arguments in its application and in particular failing to
Decision 12 - 14

adjudicate on the claim that the Respondent was not entitled to develop or work on the app
or reaching any conclusion on the issue of IP rights. It is clear, however, that the arbitrator
had no power to “resolve” these matters and could only, at the highest, grant an injunction
on an interim basis to restrain the Respondent’s conduct. That application, however, failed on
the conventional grounds discussed above and there is nothing, in my view, to indicate that
the arbitrator conducted her analysis of these issues in anything other than a diligent and
professional manner.
46. The conclusion is that the challenge amounts to an attempt to appeal or overturn the
arbitrator’s decision on the application for interim measures and in my opinion no proper
grounds are made out upon which the arbitrator’s conduct can legitimately be challenged.
The challenge must therefore be dismissed.
Second Challenge
47. The second challenge, as noted above, is said to be based in part on the arbitrator’s response
to the first challenge, in which she denied the accusations made against her both personally
and in terms of her conduct of the arbitration. The response is said to give rise to justifiable
doubts as to the arbitrator’s impartiality or independence. As a separate ground it is
contended that the arbitrator’s CV made a false and misleading statement regarding her
experience by representing that she had previously been appointed and/or acted as an
arbitrator which is asserted to be untrue.
48. As regards the response of the arbitrator to the first challenge, [Arbitrator A’s] statement is
set out above. In its submission in support of her second Challenge, the Claimant asserts that
the arbitrator’s response to a challenge “should be to assist the tribunal resolving the
challenge, not to take up the cudgels and to argue (alongside the Respondent) against the
Claimant. To do so gives the impression of lack of impartiality”. The submissions continued
in similar vein for a number of paragraphs and concluded by criticising the tone and language
of the response and particularly objecting to the fact that [Arbitrator A] states in the second
paragraph of her response “I object strongly therefore to any suggestion that I lack
competence to hear the case”. It is then pointed out that at the conclusion of the First
Decision 12 - 15

Challenge. it is stated that “the Claimant makes no personal attack on the arbitrator’s general
integrity or professionalism and does not suggest that this case should be taken as a reflection
of the arbitrator’s general ability”.
49. The Claimant’s assertion that it is not attacking the arbitrator’s “general integrity or
professionalism” is somewhat disingenuous when read against both the first challenge and
the second challenge where the Claimant seeks to pray in aid the arbitrator’s response in
defence of her reputation. In my view, the first paragraph of [Arbitrator A’s] response to the
First Challenge was measured and accurate and can be seen as a helpful re-assurance of the
arbitrator’s awareness of the requirements of impartiality when the representation of the
parties is unequal. The second paragraph, however, can be viewed as unnecessarily strident
and it may be that the arbitrator would have been wiser to have refrained from any comment
on her competence, which should be a matter which speaks for itself.
50. The claimant seeks to interpret the words “I object strongly….” as an attack on one party
indicative of partiality. In my view, it is entirely understandable that a professional whose
competence is questioned should respond in robust terms. While it would be better that the
response was not articulated, there is nothing in the arbitrator’s response to suggest that she
will be unable to continue to act in an independent and unbiased manner. In my view, the
response to the first challenge affords no grounds for the arbitrators’s removal.
51. As regards the second ground of challenge, the submission notes at paragraph 10 that the
Claimant had been informed orally by the LCIA Secretariat that this arbitration is the
arbitrator’s first appointment as arbitrator in an LCIA arbitration. The Claimant then seeks to
develop a case that the failure to state that this was the first arbitration the arbitrator had
ever undertaken (if that be the case) gives rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s
impartiality, and constitutes a breach of the Arbitration Agreement and a material
misrepresentation of the position regarding her experience. The breach of the Arbitration
Agreement arises from Article 14.5 of the LCIA Rules that requires all parties to act at all times
in good faith.
Decision 12 - 16

52. In addition to the statement at paragraph 10 of the second challenge, it may be noted that in
the First Challenge at paragraph 18 it is stated:
The Claimant has since been informed that this was [Arbitrator A’s] first appointment
in any arbitration under the LCIA Rules. […] However from [Arbitrator A’s] CV it
appears to the Claimant’s Counsel that she has been appointed in very few
arbitrations at all if any. …
At paragraph 40 of the same challenge it is stated:
It may further have been contributed to by the arbitrator’s inexperience: this was her
first ever LCIA appointment (notwithstanding it being a sole arbitrator case with a
litigant in person and a request for expedition). The arbitrator’s experience in other
fora as arbitrator was limited or non-existent.
And at paragraph 79 of the same challenge:
Furthermore the Claimant has been informed by the LCIA that this arbitration was the
arbitrator’s first appointment in an arbitration under the LCIA Rules. The Claimant
does not know whether the arbitrator had ever sat as an arbitrator in other
arbitrations, but notes that the arbitrator’s CV lists cases in which she has “been
involved either as counsel or arbitrator” but does not specifically identify any
arbitration reference in which she has been appointed for example by reference to a
seat or a set of rules.
53. It is plain that these matters were known to the Claimant from the date of [Arbitrator A’s]
appointment on 29 November 2018, or shortly thereafter. Her CV was freely available and,
the question whether [Arbitrator A] had ever sat in another arbitration, i.e. non LCIA, was
clearly a matter which had occurred to the Claimant or should have occurred to it in the light
of the statements contained in the First Challenge. Had the matter of the arbitrator’s previous
experience been regarded as relevant by the Claimant, the question should have been raised
either with the LCIA or with [Arbitrator A] herself as to whether she had ever sat as an
arbitrator. Whatever the answer, it is clear that the Claimant had the means of discovering
such information. From November 2018, the Claimant was fully aware that this was
[Arbitrator A’s] first appointment in an LCIA arbitration and that, in the Claimant’s own words,
“she has been appointed in very few arbitrations at all, if any”.
Decision 12 - 17

54. In those circumstances, the challenge is clearly barred by paragraph 10.3 of the LCIA Rules.
Given the fact that the Claimant places reliance on [Arbitrator A’s] alleged lack of experience
in the first challenge, no case could be made out for waiving the time limit and allowing the
second challenge to proceed when that challenge is issued 6 months after the date on which
the Claimant must be taken to have become aware of the ground now relied on. The second
Challenge must therefore be dismissed.
55. However, it would be wrong to dismiss the second challenge merely on a technicality. If the
matters asserted are indeed of any relevance or importance to the Claimant, it is inexplicable
why the matter was not pursued as soon as [Arbitrator A] was appointed. The implication of
the second Challenge is that it is relevant to the arbitrator’s conduct of the case that she had
not or may not have been appointed as arbitrator in any other case.
56. In my view, such an assertion could not properly ground a challenge based on Article 10.2 of
the LCIA Rules without evidence of lack of fairness or impartiality or other questionable
conduct to support the challenge. The appointment of arbitrators is a matter for the LCIA
Court who can be expected to investigate the arbitrator’s general experience and specific
experience in arbitration matters. In the case of [Arbitrator A], as her response states and as
confirmed in her CV, she has an impressive career involving wide experience […]. In addition,
her conduct of the present arbitration up to and including the application for interim relief
was entirely consistent with the requirements of the LCIA Rules of efficiency, diligence and
industry in disposing effectively of difficult and contentious issues in a cost effective manner.
Decision
For all the above reasons, both applications must be dismissed and the Claimant is ordered to
pay the costs of both applications. The Respondent is directed to submit a schedule of its costs
so that the appropriate order may be made. The arbitration costs incurred in relation to the
challenge will be determined by the LCIA Court.
